EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN ― “Do More Roads (or More Buses) Create More Traffic?”  

====================================================================  
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Chosen strategy: Two–way-fixed-effects panel Instrumental-Variables (2SLS) difference-in-differences.  

Why IV?  
• Simple panel DID (ΔVKT on Δlane-km) is subject to reverse-causality and simultaneity: places that anticipate high demand lobby for and receive more lane-km.  
• Plausibly exogenous historical “corridor endowments” exist:  
  – 1947 Interstate Highway Plan route map (never revised to anticipate post-war suburbanisation)  
  – 1898 privately built trunk railroad network  
  – 1835–50 federal exploration expedition routes  
These routes were drawn for national-defence or 19th-century commercial reasons, not to accommodate 1980-2000 metropolitan traffic. They strongly predict where new lane-km were subsequently built.  

Why panel + FE?  
• Removes time-invariant MSA heterogeneity (topography, historical settlement patterns) and common national shocks.  
• Allows us to exploit two decade windows (1983-93, 1993-2003) as quasi “events.”  

For public transit, we use an analogous instrument: the 1974 UMTA formula grants, which allocate capital subsidies principally as a fixed dollar amount per MSA population and vehicle revenue-miles in 1970. Because the formula persisted, the 1970 allocation interacts with time-varying federal transit appropriations to deliver exogenous shocks to transit vehicle supply. This is a “shift-share” (Bartik) style instrument.  

The two‐stage model:  
Stage 1: ln(lane-km)_{mt} = γ₁(period­t × pred_lanes_{m}) + δₘ + ϑ_t + W_{mt}β + u_{mt}  
Stage 2: ln(VKT)_{mt} = α·ln(ĥlane-km)_{mt} + δₘ + ϑ_t + W_{mt}β + ε_{mt}  

Same for transit with ln(bus_peak)_{mt} instrumented by formula_{m}×federal_transit_budget_{t}.  

====================================================================  
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable:  
• Primary: ln(lane-kilometres of interstate + principal urban arterial inside the urbanised portion of the MSA).  
• Secondary: ln(peak-service large buses).  

What constitutes “treated”?  
• Treated MSAs are those whose instrument-predicted corridors received disproportionately large expansions in a given decade.  

Control group:  
• MSAs with low or zero predicted construction in the same decade. Because the 2-way FE absorbs common shocks, they act as counterfactuals.  

Treatment timing / event date:  
• Two events: 1983–1993 construction boom and 1993–2003 boom. We code a dummy for each decade interacted with the historical corridor exposure.  

No RDD; running variables not used.  

====================================================================  
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance – Historical corridor exposure strongly predicts subsequent decade-level lane-km growth. Plausible because 70-80 % of new Interstate mileage followed the 1947 plan. Will test F-stats (>10).  

A2. Exclusion – 19th-century railroad / expedition lines affect 1980-2000 driving only through the roads later laid on top of them (no direct effect on contemporaneous VKT). Given the decline of inter-city passenger rail and irrelevance of exploration routes, this seems plausible but will be scrutinised.  

A3. Parallel-trends conditional on FE – In absence of road construction, high- and low-exposure MSAs would have experienced similar VKT growth. We will present pre-trend tests using 1970–83 HPMS and 1977 NPTS.  

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers between MSAs). Possibly violated by inter-MSA travel; we later cluster by BEA economic areas and test robustness excluding megaregions.  

====================================================================  
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & REMEDIES  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Endogenous migration or industrial location: historical corridor exposure might have attracted population growth, which itself raises VKT.  
 Remedy: Control for population, employment, and industry mix in W_{mt}; show results robust when instrumented lanes are normalised by population (ln(lane-km per capita)). Also estimate reduced-form impact on population to quantify this channel.  

T2. Roads built along historical corridors may coincide with geographic features (flat land) that lower driving costs irrespective of capacity.  
 Remedy: Include MSA-specific linear time trends interacted with topography; check robustness in subsample of relatively flat MSAs.  

T3. Measurement error in HPMS lane-km counts (especially in 1983 edition).  
 Remedy: Instrument alleviates attenuation; additionally, re-classify lane-km using sum of counties within MSA and compare against FHWA statistics.  

====================================================================  
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ------------- 0. Packages -------------
library(data.table)     # fast load/merge
library(fixest)         # for fast 2SLS with FE
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# ------------- 1. Load data -------------
hpms   <- fread("hpms_83_93_03.csv")   # lane km, AADT, VKT
npts   <- fread("npts_95_01.csv")      # household & commute outcomes
buses  <- fread("fta_sec15_84_94_04.csv")
corr   <- fread("historical_corridor_exposure.csv")  # share of route miles per MSA
pop    <- fread("cbp_population.csv")

# ------------- 2. Construct panel -------------
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("msa","year"), all=TRUE),
                list(hpms, buses, pop, corr))

# keep target years
panel <- panel[year %in% c(1983,1993,2003)]

# decade indicator
panel[, period := factor(fifelse(year==1993,"p83_93",
                          fifelse(year==2003,"p93_03","baseline")))]

# logged variables
panel[, ln_lane := log(lane_km_interstate_urban)]
panel[, ln_VKT  := log(VKT_urban)]
panel[, ln_bus  := log(peak_buses)]
panel[, ln_pop  := log(population)]

# ------------- 3. First-stage variables -------------
# Interstate plan exposure (time-invariant)
# Build interaction with period dummies
panel[, instr_83_93 := corridor_share*(period=="p83_93")]
panel[, instr_93_03 := corridor_share*(period=="p93_03")]

# Same for transit formula
panel[, tr_instr_84_94 := transit_formula74*(period=="p83_93")]
panel[, tr_instr_94_04 := transit_formula74*(period=="p93_03")]

# ------------- 4. 2SLS estimation -------------
# Main roads specification
iv_main <- feols(ln_VKT ~ 1 | msa + year ~ ln_lane | instr_83_93 + instr_93_03,
                 data = panel, cluster = "msa")
summary(iv_main)

# ------------- 5. Robustness: per-capita & pre-trend test -------------
panel[, ln_lane_pc := log(lane_km_interstate_urban/population)]
panel[, ln_VKT_pc  := log(VKT_urban/population)]

iv_pc <- feols(ln_VKT_pc ~ 1 | msa + year ~ ln_lane_pc |
                         instr_83_93 + instr_93_03,
               data = panel, cluster="msa")
summary(iv_pc)

# Pre-trend (1970-83) placebo
hpms70 <- fread("hpms_70.csv")
placebo <- merge(hpms70, corr, by="msa")
placebo[, ln_lane70 := log(lane_km_1970)]
placebo[, ln_VKT70  := log(VKT_1970)]
placebo[, ln_lane83 := log(lane_km_1983)]
placebo[, ln_VKT83  := log(VKT_1983)]
placebo[, dln_VKT := ln_VKT83 - ln_VKT70]
placebo[, dln_lane:= ln_lane83 - ln_lane70]

ols_placebo <- feols(dln_VKT ~ dln_lane + corridor_share, data=placebo)
summary(ols_placebo)
# expect small / insignificant coefficient
```

====================================================================  
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory (induced-demand): one new lane-km produces roughly one new vehicle-km per year in the medium run (elasticity ≈ 1). Therefore:  

• Anticipated IV elasticity of ln(VKT) w.r.t. ln(lane-km) ≈ 0.8–1.2.  
• For transit, we expect a modest negative effect on VKT (elasticity −0.1 to −0.3) because rail-oriented commuters are a small share of total traffic and bus lanes may even add to congestion if poorly utilised.  

====================================================================  
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (for 2SLS panel)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Relevance (first-stage F>10) ……………………………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion (no direct path from instrument to outcome) ………. 0.5  
C3: Parallel trends / no differential shocks after FE ……………… 0.5  
C4: No SUTVA violations / limited spillovers …………………… 0.5  
C5: Correct functional form & robust standard errors …………… 1  

Total ≈ 3.5 / 5.
